blocks.text: In a Lagos market, garri sits with garri and pepper with pepper — you find what you need because things are grouped. Biologists face the same problem on an enormous scale: nearly two million named species. Classification is the market layout that makes life findable.

blocks.markdown:
## Taxonomy and the hierarchy

**Taxonomy** is the science of naming and classifying organisms. Modern classification is **hierarchical**: large groups contain smaller groups, and organisms in the smaller groups share more features.

The ranks, from the largest to the smallest, are:

**K**ingdom → **P**hylum (Division in plants) → **C**lass → **O**rder → **F**amily → **G**enus → **S**pecies

A mnemonic Nigerian students often use is *King Placed Cows Over Female Goats Softly*. As you move down the list the number of organisms in each group falls but the number of shared features rises.

blocks.title: Species
blocks.text: A group of organisms so similar that they can interbreed freely to produce fertile offspring. This is the smallest and most precise unit of classification. A horse and a donkey can breed, but the mule they produce is sterile, so they are different species.

blocks.caption: Humans and cats share the same kingdom, phylum and class but diverge at order — so they are more closely related to each other than either is to maize

blocks.markdown:
### Binomial nomenclature

Carolus Linnaeus gave every species a two-word Latin name. The rules are strict and examiners test them:

1. The **first word is the genus**, and it begins with a **capital letter**.
2. The **second word is the species**, and it begins with a **small letter**.
3. The whole name is *italicised* in print, or **underlined** when handwritten.

So the correct forms are *Homo sapiens*, *Zea mays*, *Escherichia coli*, *Plasmodium falciparum*. Writing *homo Sapiens* or *Homo Sapiens* is wrong.

A scientific name works everywhere. What one language calls *efo*, another calls *ugu* and a third calls spinach, but *Telfairia occidentalis* means exactly one plant to a botanist anywhere in the world.

blocks.caption: The five kingdoms

blocks.title: Placing an unfamiliar organism
blocks.prompt: An organism is multicellular, has no chlorophyll, is made of thread-like filaments with a wall containing chitin, and feeds on dead cassava peels. Which kingdom does it belong to, and what is its mode of nutrition?

steps.text: It is multicellular and eukaryotic, so it is not in Monera and not in Protista.
It has no chlorophyll, so it cannot photosynthesise and is not in Plantae.
It has a cell wall, but animals have no cell wall, so it is not in Animalia.
A body of filaments (hyphae) with a chitin wall and no chlorophyll is the defining description of Fungi.
Feeding on dead organic matter, in this case dead cassava peels, is saprophytic nutrition.

blocks.answer: It belongs to the kingdom Fungi and its nutrition is saprophytic.

blocks.title: Classification reflects relatedness
blocks.text: Modern classification is not just tidy filing. Organisms are grouped by shared ancestry, so the more ranks two organisms share, the more recently they had a common ancestor. This is why classification is used as evidence for evolution.

blocks.title: Marks lost cheaply
blocks.text: In any question that asks for a scientific name, underline it and capitalise only the genus. Candidates who know the organism perfectly still lose the mark for writing 'zea Mays'.

points: The taxonomic hierarchy runs kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
A species is a group whose members interbreed to give fertile offspring.
Binomial names have a capitalised genus and a lower-case species, italicised or underlined.
The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Groups reflect shared ancestry, so classification is itself evidence of evolutionary relationship.
